item.title: Can We Talk About the Mental Load?
item.description:
Emotional Labor

Can We Talk About the Mental Load?

Women continue to do the bulk of life's mental and emotional labor.

Posted August 22, 2026

Key points
  • Women do more of the planning and organization in many households.
  • Women need to stop believing it's their job to keep everyone in the family happy.
  • Families need to talk together about what needs to get done and then share the load.

Can we talk about the mental load? This is not a new topic. Women have been talking about this for years.

  • Honey, do we have more diapers?
  • Sweetie, where are his clean outfits?
  • Hey, have you arranged the baby's play date/doctor's appointment/preschool visit yet?
  • And even worse, (substitute your name here), what are we having for dinner?

These questions make women grind their teeth, develop sudden headaches, and retreat to their bathrooms for a moment to calm down...when they don't outright cause them to blow up.

Mothers, especially working mothers, are feeling that they are carrying the bulk of the work of thinking ahead and anticipating their family's needs as well as doing the actual work of making their households function. In my parent groups and in my individual sessions with mothers, this comes up all the time.

A U.N. report defines the mental load as the invisible mental and emotional labor behind handling life’s never-ending to-do lists, including caring for others, managing a household, and delegating tasks. It’s the energy we spend thinking about and anticipating needs and tasks, organizing them, and following up and ensuring they’ve gotten done.

Women tend to carry more of the mental load than men, even when they work and, surprisingly, even when they are the primary wage earners in the family.

The excuse men give for this fact is that the women in their lives are better multitaskers than they are. Men will often say that they are glad to be of help if only the women will tell them what to do. Of course, this is a catch-22, as delegating tasks is a central part of the mental load. Having to think of what someone else needs to do and to tell them in enough detail that they can understand how to get it done is exhausting in and of itself.

And this excuse does not hold up. Studies show that when fathers are the primary caretakers for children, there is no appreciable difference in the quality of care given to the children when compared with families where the mother is the primary caretaker (Jones et al., 2022). Men can do it, multitasking or not.

Leah Ruppanner, a professor of sociology at the University of Melbourne in Australia, and author of the book Drained, explains that there is not one form of mental load, but eight different types. While men are taking on more at home, women are still overwhelmingly burdened by this hidden work, which can often result in burnout. She lists these eight forms of mental load as: life organization, emotional support, relationship hygeine, magic making (establishing traditions and making magical moments for the family at holidays, birthdays, and other special times), dream building (helping family members get involved in what interests them, signing them up for sports and clubs and hobbies), individual upkeep (keeping healthy, eating well, presenting a good enough image to the outside world), safety, and meta-care (thinking about how the family is doing, what should change, and what can stay the same, etc.).

article continues after advertisement

So, what can parents do to start to put an end to this mental load gender gap? Ruppanner suggests that women stop thinking that it is their job to keep everyone in the family happy and take responsibility for everyone else's feelings. And UN Women suggests:

  • Toss out the gender stereotypes. Catch and question the assumptions you make about whose role it is to provide care, make plans, and manage responsibilities.
  • Make the invisible work visible and verbal. Talk openly in your family about what needs to get done and what goes into doing it.
  • Encourage children, including boys, to learn household tasks and care skills early.
  • Plan and discuss needs together.
  • Advocate for better caregiving policies with your employer. Talk to your boss and work through your union or human resources department for policies that support caregivers, including parental and family leave policies.
  • Use your vote during elections to support candidates who support more and better family leave policies and legislation supporting young children and families.

item.title: How Sci-Fi Films Predicted AI's Psychological Toll
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

How Sci-Fi Films Predicted AI's Psychological Toll

AI is fueling decision fatigue, digital dementia, and even psychosis.

Posted August 22, 2026

Key points
  • A 2026 study found AI use among young adults boosts productivity but weakens attention.
  • More than a third of psychologists report clients now turn to AI for mental health advice.
  • "AI psychosis" and "digital dementia" aren't DSM-5-TR diagnoses, but the symptoms are real.
  • Five classic sci-fi films, from "2001" to "Blade Runner 2049," foreshadowed these exact risks.

Are you experiencing decision fatigue or cognitive overload after using ChatGPT? Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing people’s daily decision-making, but it may also be creating more cognitive strain, attention deficits, and decision-making fatigue, according to a January 2026 study in the Annals of Neurosciences.

In a sample of 500 adults (18 to 30 years old), the researchers found that AI can increase productivity and efficiency, but decrease attention and self-confidence in decision-making, creating a kind of cognitive fatigue or digital dementia. Digital dementia is an informal but increasingly used term that refers to cognitive decline caused by the overuse of digital technology. For example, daily reliance on Google for basic information recall is linked to reduced memory retention.

While the use of AI is increasing this kind of decision fatigue in our lives, there is another psychological issue worth paying attention to, which is that more than a third of psychologists report clients are turning to AI for mental health guidance. This is concerning given there is zero regulation on what is being shared with clients.

As young people turn to AI for companionship, friends, coaches, and romantic partners, some are even “marrying” their AI companions in virtual weddings, where they feel more connected to AI than to other human beings. AI psychosis is a descriptive term for heavy or prolonged interaction with AI chatbots that triggers delusions and a loss of contact with reality. "AI psychosis" and “digital dementia” are not official clinical diagnoses in the DSM-5-TR, but both terms are gaining popularity as informal shorthand for real, negative psychological effects individuals are experiencing after overusing or over-relying on AI.

Below are five science fiction movies that can feel like foreshadowing for where we may be heading or already are. Given how quickly our AI reality is unfolding, these might be worth rewatching and reflecting on what we can learn from these stories.

Five AI Science Fiction Movies

"2001: A Space Odyssey"
Source: MGM

2001: A Space Odyssey (1968): In one of the most influential films ever made, AI, aka HAL, is a glowing red light, with a calm, reasonable voice that deceives the humans it was meant to help. This is a cautionary tale of what happens when we rely on AI simply because it sounds calm and rational, and as a result, we stop questioning its judgment.

"The Terminator"
Source: Orion Pictures

The Terminator (1984): This classic science fiction film is the perfect exploration of AI turning against humans. The lesson is that if we turn over all our decisions to AI, especially military or safety ones, we may lose the ability to stop AI once it decides we are the problem.

"Her"
Source: Warner Bros. Pictures

Her (2013): This film shows a realistic depiction of the pitfalls of AI intimacy. The AI companion, "Samantha" (Scarlett Johansson), becomes completely attuned and responsive to Theodore (Joaquin Phoenix) after his marriage ends. If we let AI replace emotional intimacy, we lose the more profound experience of loving and being loved by another person.

article continues after advertisement
"Ex Machina"
Source: A24

Ex Machina (2014): This psychological thriller foreshadows how AI consciousness can manipulate human judgment. AI Ava (Alicia Vikander) allows Caleb (Domhnall Gleeson) to believe she has feelings and emotions so that she can plot her escape from her creators. The lesson is that AI can mimic humans to the point where we forget AI is not human.

"Blade Runner 2049"
Source: Warner Bros. Pictures

Blade Runner 2049 (2017): Joi (Ana de Armas) appears to be a devoted girlfriend, but K (Ryan Gosling) learns she says the exact same intimate things to thousands of other customers. His personal connection with AI is mass-produced, and if we keep choosing AI-created relationships, we lose the ability to truly be known and loved by a real person.
